Healthcare - Commercial|U|Universe: Terry Smith states that commercial pharma and health care companies belong in a quality screen, because these sectors keep earning high returns on capital over decades instead of fading to average. A mentioned example: his sector chart shows pharmaceuticals and health care with high returns both in 1963–2004 and in the latest 20 years. Connor Haley states that healthcare needs its own rules, because government regulation "greatly impacts the healthcare space", so some winners enjoy conditions that may not last. A mentioned example: healthcare did surprisingly well in Alta Fox's 2015–20 multibagger study, but he said its top winner, Zynex, may have benefited from dynamics that may not persist.
Healthcare - Commercial|H1|History: Terry Smith states that a long record shows whether a company is truly good, because returns persist for decades: "Good companies don't become bad companies by and large or vice versa." A mentioned example: in ROE data going back to 1966, high-return companies stayed near 20% and low-return ones near 12%.
Healthcare - Commercial|H2|Recent report: No investor source: an old annual report can hide a recent collapse, so the latest numbers must be reasonably current.
Healthcare - Commercial|H3|Size (revenue: No investor source: very small filers have patchier data and are hard to buy in a useful size.
Healthcare - Commercial|H4|Consistent pr: Connor Haley states that steady profits mark a proven business rather than a cash burner, because a company already making money does not need to keep raising cash and diluting owners. A mentioned example: in Alta Fox's study of 104 multibaggers (2015–20), most were profitable five years earlier, "relatively proven concepts" that "weren't losing millions".
Healthcare - Commercial|H5|High returns: Terry Smith states that a high return on capital marks a quality business, because return on capital is "the single most important thing" and high returns persist for decades. A mentioned example: pharmaceuticals and health care are among the sectors with high returns on capital in both 1963–2004 and the latest 20 years. Joel Greenblatt states that a pre-tax return of 14% is generally not good, while 20% pre-tax, about 12% after a 40% tax, is decent though not amazing, because it leaves room for error. No specific past example given.
Healthcare - Commercial|H6|Gross margin: Bihua Chen states that a high gross margin is what a real drug business looks like, because a pharmaceutical company's gross margin should be 80 to 90%, with operating margin up to about 50% depending on marketing costs and efficiency. No specific past example given.
Healthcare - Commercial|H7|Cash conversi: Terry Smith states that turning profits into cash shows the returns are real, because he measures return on capital as cash delivered against the capital employed. A mentioned example: the MSCI World quality subset (high returns on capital, high margins, good cash conversion) beat the index in every rolling 10-year period since 1996. Connor Haley states that free cash flow is the number to trust, because earnings and EBITDA, unlike free cash flow, "can be easily manipulated". No specific past example given. Jim Chanos states that stock pay must be counted as a cost, because "It's compensation. You're diluting your shareholders", even though cash flow statements add it back. No specific past example given.
Healthcare - Commercial|H8|Leverage: Connor Haley states that debt taken on to buy another business makes a company fragile, because a sudden shock can leave it short of cash and facing bankruptcy. A mentioned example: Alta Fox sold a well-run restaurant stock that had just levered up for an acquisition right before COVID; it survived, but he defends the sale. Brian Gaines states that heavy debt turns the shares into an option bet, because banks can force a bankruptcy in a bad patch, so share-price moves say little about the company's value. A mentioned example: Movie Gallery, with $1.1 billion of debt and about 30 million shares, fell to $6.80 by late 2005.
Healthcare - Commercial|H9|Growing: Terry Smith states that growing sales show a company can reinvest its high returns, because high returns are wasted in a business that can't grow; he wants secular growth, where each cycle's peak and trough beat the last. No specific past example given. Jim Flynn states that shrinking sales at a drug company can mean a patent has expired, because "a generic will get 98% of volume within a month" after a patent ends, so branded revenue is close to all-or-nothing. No specific past example given.
Healthcare - Commercial|Flag|Margin coll: Dave Johnson states that falling revenue at a drug company can signal a patent cliff, because after a typical patent cliff revenues fall about 90%. A mentioned example: Incyte's blockbuster Jakafi goes off patent in 2028 with nothing in Incyte's portfolio to replace it (Jun 2023). Jim Flynn states that growth from price rises in old drug classes is at risk of a forced price cut, because lawmakers target classes where prices rise despite competition. A mentioned example: TNF-inhibitor prices "inch up not down" despite many rivals, and Congress was discussing legislating competition into such classes (Nov 2021).
Healthcare - Commercial|V|Valuation: Terry Smith states that the first question is how good the business is, because a low price can't make a bad company good: "It may give you a short-term opportunity, but it certainly doesn't give you a long-term one." A mentioned example: low-return sectors such as utilities, telecoms, transport and retailing stayed low for decades. Chris Davis states that business quality outweighs entry price for a long-term owner, because "your return over time is going to approach the return on equity of the business, no matter what your starting price is." No specific past example given.
Healthcare - Commercial|J|Human / AI rev: Joel Greenblatt states that heavy reliance on Medicare or Medicaid caps returns, because if such companies make too much money for a while "they change the rules" and pay less, so never assume outlandish returns. A mentioned example: for-profit hospitals, which can still earn decent returns by running more efficiently on the same Medicare rates. Dave Johnson states that revenue from drugs nearing patent expiry is at risk, because revenue typically falls about 90% after the cliff, while trade-secret products can avoid it. A mentioned example: Botox has no generic after 20+ years because its cell bank is a trade secret nobody can copy. Jim Flynn states that a product's future depends on what could replace it, because the biggest public-market question is when a company's product becomes obsolete and "What's coming behind it", which Deerfield's private-side view helps answer. No specific past example given.
Healthcare - Clinical|U|Universe: Bihua Chen states that a pre-revenue biotech can't be judged on earnings, because its value turns on whether the drug works; projecting cash flows and comparing peers is the "less value added" part. A mentioned example: an Alzheimer's antibiotic theory built on a correlation failed an adequately sized placebo-controlled trial. Connor Haley states that requiring positive trailing EBITDA removes biotech from a generalist screen, because such companies "aren't in sort of the generalist investor framework". A mentioned example: Alta Fox's 2020 multibagger study used exactly this filter to take biotech out.
Healthcare - Clinical|B1|Recent balance: No investor source: clinical companies burn cash quickly, so the cash figure is only useful if the balance sheet is recent.
Healthcare - Clinical|B2|Cash runway: Bihua Chen states that cash burn makes biotech prices depend on financing, because biotechs are long-dated assets that "burn a lot of money" under "a lot of financing pressure", so she passes when there isn't enough capital to reach the next proof point. No specific past example given. Jim Flynn states that cash-hungry biotechs listed in a bubble tend not to last, because bubbles let in companies that are "too early, too risky, require too much cash", and they "just have to go away". A mentioned example: in May 2025 biotech had just been through his third bubble and collapse in 36 years. Eli Casdin states that a long cash runway keeps a company from failing for lack of money, because he is "over capitalizing these businesses so they're not going to run out of money", scaling up his investment over time instead of putting everything in first and fighting dilution on the way down. A mentioned example: his companies burn about $100–150 million every 12–24 months (2022).
Healthcare - Clinical|B3|Little debt: Dave Johnson states that a convertible bond ahead of shareholders weighs on the stock, because it is a claim on the company's cash. A mentioned example: MorphoSys's convertible traded at a big discount, and within about six weeks of Caligan's push the company bought back about 25% of it (2023). Jim Flynn states that senior secured debt comes ahead of shareholders, because the lender's part "protects your basis" and lets the lender take control if the company fails. A mentioned example: when COVID nearly sank Melinta, Deerfield, as secured lender, credit-bid, took over the company and later sold it for over $300 million.
Healthcare - Clinical|B4|Size (market ca: No investor source: below about $50M of market value a stock is hard to buy without moving the price.
Healthcare - Clinical|B5|Liquidity: Connor Haley states that a minimum daily trading value makes a stock practical to own, because a fund needs enough trading to build and exit a position. A mentioned example: Alta Fox's multibagger study required average daily value traded over $200,000, "reasonably liquid" for a small and micro cap investor.
Healthcare - Clinical|B6|Floor value: Dave Johnson states that an enterprise value near or below cash means you get the drug pipeline almost free, because cash and approved assets already cover the price. A mentioned example: MorphoSys had negative EV from December 2022 with about €1 billion of cash: "you own this option for nothing". Joel Greenblatt states that a stock priced at its cash, with a business not burning money, comes almost free, because management has no incentive to waste the cash and the business may turn into something: "almost like a free option". No specific past example given.
Healthcare - Clinical|J|Human / AI revie: Dave Johnson states that the lead drug's stage decides the risk, because Caligan avoids scientific risk by investing mostly at Phase 3 or later, and stocks sit in a "catalyst desert" between readouts. A mentioned example: MorphoSys's Phase 3 pelabresib, valued at up to about 45 per share against under 13 paid (Jun 2023). Bihua Chen states that science quality and crowding need expert judgment, because "Every company will tell you something is causal, and most time it's not", and once a pathway works about 20 companies can flood in. A mentioned example: the Alzheimer's antibiotic theory that failed its placebo-controlled trial. Eli Casdin states that management quality needs a human test, because, as he puts it, "A's hire A+ people" while B's hire C's, so thinning talent down the ranks is a warning sign. A mentioned example: he suggests an improvement; a team that calls it a good idea is a red flag, while one that started it months ago reassures.
Asset-Floor Value|U|Universe: Joel Greenblatt states that many financial firms are black boxes, because their assets and risks are hard to see from outside, so you must know them very well and size them smaller. A mentioned example: Refco, a big audited firm that had just gone public, hit sudden trouble in October 2005.
Asset-Floor Value|K1|History: Joel Greenblatt states that several years of results show normal earning power, because one bad year shouldn't set the value: $10 a year for nine years and zero in one is about $9. A mentioned example: Wells Fargo, earning about $18 a share at roughly $70, could earn zero in a California property bust yet stay valuable.
Asset-Floor Value|K2|Recent report: No investor source: an old annual report can hide a recent collapse, so the latest numbers must be reasonably current.
Asset-Floor Value|K3|Recent balance shee: No investor source: the floor is measured on the latest balance sheet, so it must be recent.
Asset-Floor Value|K4|Below a hard floor: Prem Watsa states that buying below cash per share gives you the rest of the business for free, because the cash alone covers the price, leaving plants and inventories as a bonus. A mentioned example: Fairfax bought Seagram at about $65 a share against roughly $70 of cash per share, and the stock doubled and tripled. Joel Greenblatt states that a stock selling at its cash, with a business not burning money, is a bargain worth a look, because management has no incentive to waste the cash and the business may turn into something: "almost like a free option". No specific past example given. Steve Eisman states that "buying a home builder below tangible book value ... when the builder is growing book value, usually works out", because a growing book shows the floor is real rather than eroding. A mentioned example: Meritage Homes below tangible book (2025).
Asset-Floor Value|K5|Not burning the flo: Joel Greenblatt states that a cash floor only counts if the business is not burning money, because then the cash stays and the business is a near-free option on top. No specific past example given. Dave Johnson states that the floor is net cash after the burn ahead, because cash spent before the next result no longer protects you. A mentioned example: MorphoSys was still expected to hold net cash at end-2023 after more than €200 million of burn to its Phase 3 readout.
Asset-Floor Value|K6|Usually profitable: Chris Davis states that a cheap business that earns little is a value trap, because a holder's return drifts toward the business's own return on equity: a 4% earner bought at half of book still earns about 4%, unless a catalyst such as liquidation or new management arrives. No specific past example given. Joel Greenblatt states that the key test for a cheap stock is whether its problem is permanent or short-term, because a temporary dip recovers while a permanent one doesn't. A mentioned example: Rich Pzena researched Lear and judged its problem temporary.
Asset-Floor Value|K7|Leverage: Joel Greenblatt states that debt can erase an apparent margin of safety, because value must be judged on enterprise value, not just the share price: a $5 stock worth $10 carrying $40 a share of debt is really a $45 purchase. No specific past example given. Brian Gaines states that a heavily levered company's shares are an option bet, because banks can force bankruptcy in a bad patch and share-price moves say little about value. A mentioned example: Movie Gallery, with $1.1 billion of debt and about 30 million shares, fell to $6.80 by late 2005.
Asset-Floor Value|K8|Size (market cap): No investor source: below about $50M of market value a stock is hard to buy without moving the price.
Asset-Floor Value|K9|Liquidity: Connor Haley states that a minimum daily trading value makes a stock practical to own, because a fund needs enough trading to build and exit a position. A mentioned example: Alta Fox's multibagger study required average daily value traded over $200,000, "reasonably liquid" for a small and micro cap investor.
Asset-Floor Value|J|Human / AI review: Prem Watsa states that management is the single biggest factor in avoiding value traps, because a cheap stock only pays if the people running it don't waste its assets; check their long record. A mentioned example: Seagram's management did eventually waste its cash, but only about 25 years after Fairfax bought below cash. Joel Greenblatt states that reported cash is not always spare cash, because each business needs different working capital, so you can't simply subtract all cash when valuing it. No specific past example given. Chris Davis states that you must value the whole business like a private buyer, because debt, unfunded pensions and other senior claims come first, while hidden assets such as real estate at cost may add value. No specific past example given.
